name: Zigni
subtitle: Zigni is a traditional Eritrean stew of beef or chicken and vegetables in a spicy, tomato-based sauce seasoned with berbere.

facts.label: Main ingredients
facts.value: Beef or chicken with vegetables and a hot spice blend called berbere, simmered for a long time.

facts.label: When it is eaten
facts.value: A traditional Eritrean dish served at parties and family gatherings.

facts.label: What it is
facts.value: A spicy tomato-based sauce served with any protein.

facts.label: How it is eaten
facts.value: Traditionally eaten with injera, a spongy flatbread made from fermented batter.

facts.label: Spices
facts.value: Berbere contains aromatic spices such as cinnamon, cumin, cardamom and fenugreek.

parts.text: Zigni is a traditional Eritrean stew of beef or chicken and vegetables in a spicy, tomato-based sauce seasoned with berbere. The berbere blend includes spices such as cinnamon, cumin, cardamom and fenugreek, and the stew is simmered for a long time.
It is traditionally eaten with injera, a spongy flatbread from fermented batter, and is served at parties and family gatherings.

blocks.title: Zigni berbere (beef)
blocks.sub: One version of the dish, as given by Great British Chefs; the steps are summarised in our own words. Recipes differ from cook to cook.
blocks.note: Quantities are the source's own; the page lists 6 servings and 1 hour 50 minutes in total. Sauté time is given as 5-8 minutes.

steps.text: Season the beef with salt and pepper and brown it all over in 2 tbsp of the oil on high heat; lift it out.
Lower the heat, add the rest of the oil and soften the onion, pepper, ginger and garlic together with the berbere.
Stir in the tomato purée and cook it briefly.
Put the beef back with the chopped tomatoes and stock, cover and simmer very gently.
Uncover and simmer until the sauce has thickened and the beef is tender.
Adjust the seasoning and serve hot, with injera, flatbread or rice.

gaps: The description is summarised from the sources listed here and should be read against them.
Not found in a readable source: Sources disagree on the grain of Eritrean injera (sorghum per Arab News, teff per The Caterer), so injera grain was not recorded.
